reading.rtitle: The Email You Write Before the AI
paras: Patricia Gomes reviews about forty emails a week from the accountants on her team, and she can tell in two lines which ones were written by a person and which ones were pasted from a machine. The machine emails are not wrong. They are just long, polite in every sentence, and strangely empty. I hope this email finds you well. I am reaching out to kindly inform you that... By the third line, the auditor has stopped reading.

The emails she likes have four parts, and the reader can see them. First, the opening, which says why you are writing: Further to our call this morning, or Regarding the Q3 accruals. Second, the core message, in one or two direct sentences. Third, the detail: the number, the date, the file you attach. And last, the close, which says what you need and by when: Could you please confirm receipt by Friday? Four parts, often fewer than a hundred words.

The hardest sentence, she says, is the one that delivers a problem to an auditor. You cannot be vague, and you cannot sound guilty. The answer is a careful sentence: It appears that the accrual was posted twice. There may be a difference in account 4100. These words do not hide the problem. They say that you found it, that you are checking it, and that you will act accordingly. It is how professionals inform people of bad news in writing.

Her advice to the team is simple. Write the draft yourself, before you open any tool. Read it aloud once. Proofread it for the four parts, not only for the grammar. Then, if you want, ask the AI to check it. The email that comes back will still be yours, and the next time you have to say the same thing in a call, you will already know the words.

listenings.text: I am an external auditor, and during an audit I read about two hundred emails from the client. I can tell you which ones I answer first. They tell me in the first line why they are writing. Regarding your question about the March adjustment. Then one sentence with the answer, and the file is attached. If something is still pending, they say so, and they give me a date. The emails I leave for later are the long ones, with three paragraphs of thank you and hope you are well before I find the information. And the ones that worry me are the vague ones. If there is a problem, I would much rather read: it appears that the entry was posted twice, we are checking it, and we will confirm by Thursday. That sentence does not scare me. It tells me the client found it first.

For two years, I wrote every email in Spanish and asked the AI to translate it. It worked, and the emails were perfect. Then one day the director called me, right after I sent an update, and asked me two questions about it. I could not answer in English. I did not know the words, because I had never really written them. So I changed one thing. Now I write the draft myself, in English, even if it is slow and not perfect. I read it out loud once. Then I ask the AI to check it, and I look at every change it makes. My emails take ten minutes longer. But when the director calls, the words are already in my mouth.
